title: Nettie and Clover's Bridge of Poems
markdown:
The wind had a way of singing through the terraced gardens of Witch Nettie’s mountain home. It carried the scent of thyme and rock-daisies, a good honest smell, the kind that makes you feel right at home. Nettie, with her silver hair pulled back in a sensible bun and spectacles perched on her nose, was kneeling amongst her plants, humming a tuneless little song that sounded like bees buzzing — or perhaps a teapot that had forgotten its manners. Beside her, curled on a sun-warmed stone like a furry spiky doughnut, was Clover. A hedgehog, yes, but a hedgehog with more sense and loyalty than many a grand sorcerer. He was Nettie’s shadow, her quiet confidante.

Nettie loosened the soil around a cluster of bright green leaves. The leaves had a silvery sheen, like they had been kissed by moonlight. Clover twitched his nose in his sleep. Nettie chuckled, a sound like dry leaves rustling. She gestured with a soil-stained finger towards a tiny sprig of mint. “A pinch of this can soothe a tummy ache, and it smells heavenly. Who would have thought such a small thing could be so grand?”

Her magic was quiet, practical, and always useful. Her fame rested on the most soothing salves, the most warming teas, the most comfortable charms to keep drafty huts snug and lost socks found. Today she needed a very particular herb — Moonpetal, for a balm that soothed away weary aches and grumbles. It was known for its silvery leaves and its ability to calm even the most fidgety of bones.

But as she reached for a delicate silver-veined leaf, a tiny sound, like a whisper of paper tearing, reached her ears. Nettie’s head snapped up, her spectacles sliding down her nose. Clover was no longer asleep. He was sitting up, looking rather pleased with himself, a small guilty nibble mark clearly visible on the very stem of the last precious Moonpetal shoot.

“Clover,” Nettie exclaimed, more in surprise than anger. Clover squeaked, looking up with wide dark eyes that seemed to say it was not him. “You have eaten the only Moonpetal I had.” Nettie sighed, but a little smile played on her lips. He was too cute to be truly cross with.

Instead of despair, a thoughtful frown creased her brow. She smoothed her apron. “Well. There is no use fretting over spilled milk, or nibbled herbs, as the case may be. The world is a big place, and mountains have secrets. If we need more Moonpetal, we must go and find it.”

Her gaze drifted towards the jagged peaks that clawed at the sky like grumpy old giants. The Whispering Peaks. A place of steep cliffs, hidden springs, and, unfortunately, the Toll Bridge of Gribble. And Gribble was a goblin postmaster of unparalleled bureaucratic zeal, known far and wide for his love of forms, stamps, and rules, rules, rules.

“Right then, Clover,” Nettie said, standing up and dusting off her worn apron. She picked up her sturdy walking stick, its wood smoothed by years of use. “We are off on an adventure. Pack your bravest spirit, little one.” Clover puffed out his chest.

As Nettie prepared her satchel with a flask of dandelion tea, a chunk of cheese wrapped in wax paper, and a warm woolly scarf, she thought about Clover. He had not always been so bold. When she had found him, a tiny trembling ball of spikes under a thorny bramble bush, he had flinched at every shadow and rustle. But Nettie had simply left out a crumb of biscuit each day, spoken softly, and never pushed. Slowly he had grown to trust her, to follow her everywhere, his little snout always nudging her hand for a gentle scratch behind his ears.

They climbed higher, the air growing thin and crisp, tasting like pure mountain spring water. The path narrowed, a ribbon of grey stone etched into the mountainside. Mist, like ethereal grey silk, began to unfurl from the fir trees below the skeletal remains of an ancient tower. “Steady now, Clover,” Nettie murmured, as a gust of wind whipped around them. Clover, trotting diligently beside her, would sometimes stop, his nose twitching furiously. He would nudge Nettie’s boot, steering her away from a loose stone or a slippery patch of moss. He was her living compass.

The path then led them to a babbling brook, its water chuckling over smooth stones. A cluster of vibrant sapphire-blue mushrooms pulsed with a soft inner light. Perched on the largest one sat a gnome, no bigger than Nettie’s thumb, with a beard like dandelion fluff. “Halt,” he chirped, his voice like tiny bells. “To pass the Gigglecap Grove, you must solve a riddle, or hop on one foot until sunset. What has an eye, but cannot see?” Nettie smiled. “A needle.” The gnome clapped his tiny hands. “Correct. You may pass.”

Soon they heard the distant rumble of water and, eventually, the loud creak of heavy timbers. The Toll Bridge of Gribble. It was a sturdy if somewhat wobbly construction, spanning a deep gurgling gorge. And there, presiding over it like a grumpy king on his throne, was Gribble himself. He was a stout goblin, with ears like wilting cabbage leaves and a waistcoat bulging like a startled pumpkin. He held a quill pen like a king his sceptre and, of course, a formidable stack of forms.

“Halt,” Gribble squeaked. “No crossing without proper documentation. Present your permits.”

Nettie approached, a polite smile on her lips. “Good day, Master Gribble. I am Witch Nettie, and this is my companion, Clover. We are just looking for some Moonpetal, and need to cross the pass to reach the sheltered hollow beyond the old tower.”

Gribble peered at her, his eyes like shiny black buttons. “Moonpetal, you say? Hmm.” He tapped his quill against his chin. “And have you filled out Form 7B, Declaration of Botanical Intent?” He held up a rather large intimidating piece of paper.

“Botanical Intent?” Nettie blinked. “I am a witch. I am gathering an herb for a healing balm.”

“Precisely.” Gribble jabbed his quill. “And to declare your intent, you need Form 7B. Or, failing that, perhaps Form 9G, Cross-Passage Herb Acquisition Request?” He shuffled through his papers, making them rustle like autumn leaves.

Nettie pulled a small velvet pouch from her satchel. “I have some particularly fine dried cloudberries, Master Gribble. They are quite plump and sweet. Would they suffice as payment?”

Gribble sniffed the air dramatically. “Cloudberries are delicious, Witch Nettie, but they do not satisfy the regulatory requirements for bridge passage. They are not logged in the system.” He waved a dismissive hand. “Now, where is your Form 7B?”

Other travellers, a pair of bleating mountain goats and a rather flustered marmot with a tiny satchel of his own, were also waiting, looking increasingly glum. The sky had begun to darken considerably, and a low rumble of thunder echoed through the peaks, making Clover’s spines prickle. The wind shrieked, a cold biting sound that whipped Nettie’s hair across her face. The air smelled sharply of damp earth and pine needles, and the jagged rocks underfoot felt slick and treacherous.

“But, Master Gribble,” Nettie tried again, kneeling to be closer to his eye level, “what is the purpose of these forms? They seem rather complicated for a simple herb.”

Gribble puffed out his chest. “It is all about happy bridge morale. The bridge, you see, it is ancient. It gets lonely if no one tells it it is doing a good job. It needs to feel appreciated. Form 7B ensures the appropriate level of appreciation is logged.” He patted his ample belly. “It is quite vital. For structural integrity, and all that. Happy bridge, happy travellers, happy goblin postmaster.”

Appreciation. Happy bridge morale. Nettie looked at Gribble, really looked at him, and then at Clover, who was now busily investigating a loose pebble. Her usual practical approach, her offers of tea and berries, would not work. Gribble was not interested in what was useful; he wanted to hear the feeling put into words.

As the first fat drops of rain began to fall, Nettie felt her shoulders slump. The Moonpetal patch near the ruined tower would be impossible to reach in this sudden storm, and they would have to turn back, defeated by a piece of paper. She watched Clover nudge a tiny blue wildflower with his nose, then sniff it with great interest. The little flower, so small, seemed to bring him a moment of quiet joy.

A thought, as delicate and bright as the wildflower, bloomed in Nettie’s mind. She knelt beside Gribble, who was now looking rather stern, the rain plastering his cabbage-leaf ears to his head.

“Master Gribble,” she said, her voice soft but clear, “I may not have your forms, but I have something else. Something that speaks to the heart of the mountains, and to the spirit of your magnificent bridge.” She paused, took a deep breath, and then began to recite, her voice weaving a gentle melody that seemed to calm the drumming rain. “Oh, bridge of stone, so strong and grand, that spans the gorge across the land. You carry folk, both near and far, beneath the sun, beneath the star. Your planks they creak, your ropes they sway, you make our journey bright each day. Master Gribble, with watchful eye, you keep us safe as we go by. And for this gift, so freely shown, our grateful thanks to you are known.”

She finished, her gaze steady on Gribble. The goblin blinked. His stern expression softened, then melted away like snow in spring. He looked at the bridge, then back at Nettie, a slow wide grin spreading across his face, revealing a missing tooth.

“Well, now,” he rumbled, his voice losing its squeak. “That is quite lovely. Really. Master Gribble, with watchful eye — I like that. It captures the essence, you see.” He fumbled for his ink pot. “This is far better than any Form 7B. This is true appreciation.” With a flourish, he took Nettie’s path-worn travel permit and stamped it with a large cheerful APPROVED — WITH GRATITUDE.

“On you go, then. And thank you for the poem. It really does make the bridge feel understood.”

Nettie and Clover hurried across the bridge, the rain now a steady drumming on the sturdy timbers. On the other side, nestled in a sheltered hollow not far from the ruined tower, they found it. A patch of Moonpetal, its silver leaves gleaming even in the dim light, each one perfect and untouched.

Back in her cottage, the Moonpetal safely stored in a cool dark place, Nettie gently stroked Clover’s quills. He nudged the mint sprig on the table, as if to say a small useful thing had got them home after all, and Nettie left a crumb of biscuit by his stone, the way she always had.
characters: Nettie (witch of a sensible bun and useful magic), Clover (a hedgehog of sense and loyalty), Gribble (a goblin postmaster of bureaucratic zeal)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
